A substrate transfer device includes a casing and a substrate conveying robot housed within the casing. The casing is dimensioned such that its size in a second direction is greater than its size in a first direction. The casing includes a plurality of walls that define a conveying chamber in which substrates are transferred. At least one opening is provided on one side of the conveying chamber in the first direction, allowing a substrate to be introduced into or removed from the conveying chamber.

The substrate conveying robot is arranged in the conveying chamber and includes a base, a robot arm connected to the base, a robot hand supported by the robot arm, and a controller configured to control the operation of the robot arm and the robot hand. The robot arm includes at least one robot link having a predetermined link length. The robot hand is configured to support and convey a substrate during transfer operations.

The link length of the robot arm is set to be smaller than the size of the conveying chamber, thereby allowing the robot arm to operate within the limited space of the casing. In contrast, the length of the robot hand is set to be at least as large as an effective size of the conveying chamber. As a result, the robot hand can reach a required substrate transfer position through the opening while the robot arm remains compact. This configuration enables efficient substrate transfer in a casing having an elongated shape in the second direction and a relatively reduced dimension in the first direction.

A substrate transfer device is provided for transferring substrates, such as semiconductor wafers, glass panels, or other plate-like workpieces, between processing modules, storage containers, or other apparatuses arranged around a transfer chamber. The device includes an elongated casing that defines a conveying chamber extending in a longitudinal direction. The casing is provided with a plurality of side openings through which substrates can be introduced into, or removed from, the conveying chamber. These side openings may be connected to processing units, load ports, load-lock chambers, buffer stations, or other substrate-handling equipment.

Within the conveying chamber, a substrate conveying robot is installed. The robot includes a base, an articulated arm supported by the base, a hand mounted at a distal end of the arm, and a controller that controls movement of the arm and hand. The robot is arranged so that its respective components occupy predetermined regions of the chamber. For example, the base may be positioned in a central or end region of the chamber, the arm may be configured to extend and retract within an arm-operating region, and the hand may be movable within a substrate transfer region aligned with the side openings. The controller operates the robot so that a substrate supported on the hand can be moved to and from the openings without interfering with the casing or surrounding equipment.

The substrate conveying robot is configured in relation to the size and shape of the conveying chamber. In particular, the length of a link of the robot arm is made shorter than the corresponding size of the conveying chamber. This allows the arm to rotate, fold, and extend inside the chamber without requiring a large clearance space. At the same time, the hand has a length that is at least as large as an effective chamber size, such as the usable width or reach distance within the conveying chamber. By making the hand relatively long while keeping the arm link relatively short, the device can obtain a sufficient substrate transfer stroke even though the chamber itself is narrow or otherwise spatially restricted.

With this configuration, the robot can access substrates through the side openings while remaining within the limited interior volume of the elongated casing. The shorter arm link reduces the space required for arm motion and helps prevent interference with the chamber walls. The longer hand compensates for the reduced arm length by extending the reachable range of the robot, thereby enabling the hand to project toward a desired opening and support or receive a substrate at an appropriate transfer position.

As a result, the substrate transfer device can be made compact while still maintaining reliable substrate handling performance. The arrangement is particularly useful in systems where multiple processing chambers or storage stations are disposed along the side of an elongated transfer chamber and where it is desirable to reduce the footprint of the overall apparatus. The device enables efficient transfer of substrates in a constrained chamber layout without requiring an enlarged robot chamber or an arm having long links that would increase the risk of collision or require additional operating space.

**The Importance of “When”**

The word *when* may seem small, but it has great importance in our lives. It is often not enough to know what we want to do; we also need to know when to do it. Timing can change everything. The right decision at the wrong time may not bring the results we hope for, while a simple action at the right moment can make a big difference.

When we plan our day, we think about time: when to wake up, when to work, when to rest, and when to meet others. The way we use time affects our success, health, and happiness. When people manage their time well, they often feel more organized and confident.

The question “when?” also helps us understand life events. When did something begin? When will it end? When should we take action? These questions guide us and help us make better choices.

In the end, the word *when* reminds us that time matters. The moment we choose can be just as important as the action itself.
